title: Recommender Systems
html:
Recommenders predict which items a user will like from past interactions (ratings, clicks, purchases, watch time) and item information. The core families are content-based filtering, collaborative filtering and matrix factorisation — usually combined.

ApproachIdeaStrengthWeakness
PopularityRecommend what's popular (per segment)Strong baseline, no cold start for usersNot personal; reinforces popularity
Content-basedItems similar to what the user liked, using item features (text, genre, tags)Works for new items; explainableOver-specialised; needs good item features
Collaborative filtering (neighbourhood)Users who agreed before will agree again / items liked by the same users are similarNo item features needed; finds surprising itemsCold start for new users and items; sparse data
Matrix factorisationLearn a latent vector per user and per item; score = their dot productScales, captures hidden tastesCold start; less explainable
Hybrid / two-stageCandidate generation (fast retrieval of hundreds of items) → ranking model with rich featuresIndustry standard at scaleMore components to build and monitor

Content-based: similar items

Collaborative filtering: item–item similarity

Matrix factorisation

r̂ᵤᵢ = pᵤ · qᵢ minimise Σ_(u,i observed) (rᵤᵢ − pᵤ·qᵢ)² + λ(‖pᵤ‖² + ‖qᵢ‖²)

Each user and item gets a vector of k latent factors (think “how much action / romance”). Only observed ratings enter the loss — treating missing ratings as 0 (plain SVD) would teach the model that unseen means disliked. Alternating least squares (ALS) fixes the items and solves a small ridge regression per user, then swaps:

User 0 loves A and B and dislikes D; the factors place C and E with D, so both get low predicted ratings — the recommender won't suggest them. (Raw dot products can leave the rating scale, hence the clipping; real systems also add a global mean plus user and item bias terms: r̂ = μ + bᵤ + bᵢ + pᵤ·qᵢ.)

Evaluating recommendations

MetricMeaning
Precision@k / Recall@kShare of the top-k that are relevant / share of relevant items that appear in the top-k
Hit rate@kDid at least one relevant item appear in the top-k?
MRRMean of 1 / rank of the first relevant item
NDCG@kRewards relevant items near the top with a log discount, normalised by the ideal ordering
Coverage, diversity, noveltyIs the system recommending more than the same popular items?
DCG@k = Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ relᵢ / log₂(i + 1) NDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k
  • Implicit feedback (clicks, views) is far more plentiful than ratings but has no explicit negatives — unobserved ≠ disliked; sample negatives carefully.
  • Cold start: new users → popularity, onboarding questions, context; new items → content features.
  • Split by time for offline evaluation, and confirm with an online A/B test — offline metrics only partly predict online engagement.
  • Watch feedback loops and popularity bias: the model only learns from what it chose to show.
Content-based vs collaborative filtering?

Content-based recommends items whose features resemble what the user liked — handles new items, but stays within the user's known tastes. Collaborative filtering uses the behaviour of similar users/items — needs no item features and can surprise, but suffers from cold start and sparsity. Production systems combine them.

How does matrix factorisation work for recommendations?

It represents each user and item by a low-dimensional latent vector and predicts a rating (or preference) as their dot product, learning the vectors by minimising error on observed interactions plus L2 regularisation, with ALS or SGD. Missing entries are not treated as zeros.

How do you solve the cold-start problem?

For new users: popularity or trending items, onboarding preferences, context (location, device, time), then quickly adapt to the first interactions. For new items: content features and embeddings, and deliberate exploration (e.g. bandits) to gather interactions.
